% ============================================================
% ABSTRACT
% ============================================================

\begin{abstract}
A model that judges the health of retired electric-vehicle batteries on one group may fail on the next. We propose Residual TFT-EWC, a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) trained with Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) that learns a shrunk correction to linear extrapolation of the recent capacity fade, and forecast the state of health (SOH) one to six capacity checks ahead on 606 cells from six public datasets. Every claimed difference must replicate on a second seed set. Residual TFT-EWC is the only model compared that does well both when groups arrive in sequence (level with extrapolation, 0.24--0.46 percentage points (pp) ahead of gradient boosting under the same no-storage rule, forgetting cut by two thirds) and on unseen usage conditions (0.43--0.68~pp ahead of extrapolation, 95.5\% correct reuse class, and ahead of gradient boosting on all 64 conditions of a further dataset). Gradient boosting that stores all earlier data remains best on unseen conditions; a replay memory of 40 rows per condition closes most of the gap. Intervals reach their coverage only when calibrated on held-out conditions. All results are shown through an interactive dashboard.
\end{abstract}

% KEYWORDS

Continual learning, second-life batteries, electric vehicles, state of health, battery degradation, heterogeneous batteries, catastrophic forgetting, machine learning

\section{Introduction}

A battery retired from an electric vehicle (EV) can often still serve as stationary storage, but only if its state of health (SOH) can be judged reliably. Machine-learning SOH models exist~\cite{ref1,ref2,ref3,ref4}, yet retired batteries differ in chemistry, maker, usage and temperature, so a model trained once may fail on the next group. Continual learning updates the model with each new group while keeping what it learned before. We propose Residual TFT-EWC, a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) trained with Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC).

We forecast SOH one to six capacity checks ahead, because a reuse decision depends on how a battery will age and because estimating today's SOH from cycling data lost to simply repeating the last measurement on our first dataset (\S\ref{sec:methods}). The forecast is sorted into capacity-based reuse classes (Fig.~\ref{fig:system}).

\textbf{Contributions.}
(i)~A leakage-free forecasting benchmark of 606 cells from six public datasets, with two label flaws removed.
(ii)~A comparison of continual strategies, simple forecasters and joint training on a stream of groups, on unseen groups and after first-life pretraining, reporting adaptation and forgetting.
(iii)~Residual TFT-EWC, which corrects linear extrapolation instead of replacing it: the only model compared that stays close to the best in both settings.
(iv)~Interval calibration and a replication rule (two seed sets) that every claimed difference must pass, with all results browsable in an interactive dashboard (Figs.~\ref{fig:dash-s6}, \ref{fig:dash-unseen}).

\section{Related Work}

Second-life studies (review:~\cite{ref6}) estimate the current SOH of a fixed set of batteries from partial charging~\cite{ref1}, health indicators~\cite{ref2}, impedance spectra~\cite{ref3}, bagged Gaussian process regression (GPR)~\cite{ref4} or online clustering~\cite{ref5}, with errors up to about 2.3\%; none updates its model as new groups arrive. Continual learning has predicted capacity loss~\cite{ref7} and state of charge across drive cycles~\cite{ref8}, and, closest to us, estimated second-life SOH across pulse-test conditions with replay~\cite{tao2026pcl}. Domain generalisation~\cite{ref9} and probabilistic bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) and temporal convolutional network (TCN) models~\cite{ref10} target second-life SOH without a task sequence. \textbf{Gap:} continual forecasting across heterogeneous second-life groups, with forgetting measured, reuse screening and comparison against simple forecasters and joint training, has not been tested.

\section{The Residual TFT-EWC Approach}
\label{sec:methods}

\subsection{Data}
\label{sec:data}

Six public CC~BY~4.0 datasets are used (Table~\ref{tab:data}); our parsing reproduces the published S1 reference performance test (RPT) capacities and all 843 S6 check capacities exactly. Estimating the current SOH on S1 lost to persistence (gradient boosting 1.78~pp, persistence 0.99~pp), because cycle features barely track health (median within-cell $|\rho|=0.09$); we therefore forecast, with the protocol fixed before any forecaster was fitted. Apache Spark condenses the S6 ageing cycles (132~GB, $9.0\times10^{8}$ rows) into 21 block inputs.

\subsection{Target, inputs and protocols}
\label{sec:soh}
\label{sec:task}
\label{sec:features}
\label{sec:protocols}

For cell $b$ with check capacities $C_{b,k}$ in time order~\cite{ref6,birkl2017},
\begin{equation}
  \begin{aligned}
    \mathrm{SOH}_{b,k} &= 100\,C_{b,k}/C_{b,1}\;\%,\\
    \Delta_{b,k,h} &= \mathrm{SOH}_{b,k+h} - \mathrm{SOH}_{b,k},
  \end{aligned}
  \label{eq:soh}
\end{equation}
so SOH is relative to the first valid check, and a forecast from origin $k$ predicts the change $\Delta$ over $h$ checks ($h{=}1$--3, E1; $h{=}1$--6, E2)~\cite{lim2021tft}. Errors are root-mean-square errors (RMSE) in percentage points (pp). Inputs use only what is known at the origin: SOH history, the fade rate $r_{b,k}$ (least-squares slope over the last three checks~\cite{hastie2009elements}), fixed descriptors, the planned usage until the target, and optional diagnostics (F1). Each cell's checks are cut at 60\% and 80\% into purged train, validation and test periods.

\textbf{Protocols.} \textbf{P1}, continual stream: one task per S1 cell or S6 condition, 10 task orders $\times$ 5 seeds. \textbf{P2}, unseen group: one cell or condition held out. \textbf{P3}: first-life pretraining on S7--S9, then the S6 stream.

\subsection{Model}
\label{sec:backbones}

The Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT)~\cite{lim2021tft} sees the four latest origins of a cell (Fig.~\ref{fig:arch}; 12{,}708 parameters). It learns a correction $g_\theta$ to linear extrapolation $\hat\Delta^{\mathrm{lin}}_{b,k,h} = r_{b,k}(t_{b,k+h}-t_{b,k})$, a residual hybrid~\cite{zhang2003hybrid}:
\begin{equation}
  \hat\Delta_{b,k,h} = \hat\Delta^{\mathrm{lin}}_{b,k,h} + \alpha_h\, g_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{b,k,h}),
  \label{eq:residual}
\end{equation}
where $\alpha_h\in[0,1]$ shrinks the correction (least-squares slope on calibration rows). After each task $j$, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC)~\cite{kirkpatrick2017ewc} adds
\begin{equation}
  \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\textstyle\sum_{p} F_{j,p}\,(\theta_p - \theta^{*}_{j,p})^2
  \label{eq:ewc}
\end{equation}
with the diagonal Fisher information $F_j$. Split-conformal intervals~\cite{lei2018conformal} take the calibration-error quantile per horizon.


\textbf{Comparators.} Persistence ($\hat\Delta=0$)~\cite{hyndman2006}, linear extrapolation, ridge, histogram gradient boosting (GB)~\cite{friedman2001}, a multilayer perceptron (MLP), fine-tuning, replay~\cite{rolnick2019replay} and joint training. GB is run with all earlier conditions stored (GB-ALL) and, under our no-storage rule, refitted on the latest condition (GB-LAST). V2 (post hoc) swaps EWC for replay of 40 rows per condition, a three-model ensemble and calibration before training.

\subsection{Metrics and statistics}
\label{sec:tuning}
\label{sec:metrics}

From the error matrix $R_{i,j}$ (task $j$ after step $i$)~\cite{lopezpaz2017gem} we report final average error (retention), error on the newest task (adaptation) and forgetting~\cite{chaudhry2018rwalk}; intervals by coverage and interval score~\cite{gneiting2007scoring}; reuse classes C0 $>$95, C1 90--95, C2 80--90, C3 $\le$80\%. Every follow-up was registered before it ran (supplement Table~SXII). A difference counts as ``replicated'' only if a Wilcoxon test~\cite{wilcoxon1945} with Holm correction~\cite{holm1979} is significant in both seed sets (0--4, 5--9), with the same sign and $|d|\ge0.05$~pp; below 0.05~pp in both it is ``equivalent''.

\textbf{Availability.} Python~3.11, PyTorch~2.14.1, one processor thread, deterministic seeds. Data DOIs are in the references; code, decision log, registrations, results and the dashboard: \url{https://github.com/TarunSitaraman/continual-learning-heterogeneous-second-life-ev-batteries}.
\label{sec:repro}

\subsection{Headline: both settings at once}
\label{sec:res-p1}
\label{sec:res-p2}
\label{sec:res-residual}
\label{sec:res-d25}
\label{sec:res-d26}

Table~\ref{tab:headline} and Fig.~\ref{fig:overview} give the main result. On the stream, Residual TFT-EWC is equivalent to linear extrapolation (0.32/0.31 against 0.34~pp) and beats GB-LAST by 0.24--0.46~pp. On unseen conditions it beats extrapolation by 0.43--0.68~pp; GB-ALL is better there because it stores every condition. Pretraining on 36{,}711 first-life samples did not help (+0.22~pp, replicated), and the 21 Spark inputs made the model worse.

\subsection{Continual learning and per-condition error (S1, S6)}
\label{sec:res-p3}
\label{sec:res-interp}
\label{sec:res-repro}
\label{sec:res-d24}

Fig.~\ref{fig:dash-s6} opens the S6 results up by task and condition. Over $h{=}1$--6, EWC cuts forgetting further, from 0.28/0.22 to 0.09~pp (replicated); shift-adaptive EWC and literature backbones (BiLSTM, TCN, Transformer, GPR) did not beat the residual TFT (supplement). Fig.~\ref{fig:dash-horizon} shows the gain over persistence growing with the horizon. On S1 all methods are level (0.46--0.48~pp) and every sample stays in class C0. An ablation credits the TFT's gain (0.89 to 0.40~pp) to dropping the diagnostics and adding the time between checks, not to the architecture.

\subsection{Reuse classes and intervals}
\label{sec:res-intervals}

The proposed model puts 95.5\% of held-out S6 samples in their measured reuse class (extrapolation 93.9\%, GB-ALL 97.7\%), and every error is off by one class only (classification metrics: supplement Table~SXV). Interval coverage holds only when calibrated on held-out conditions and fails out of range (Fig.~\ref{fig:dash-unseen}a).

\subsection{Many unseen conditions (S7, S10)}
\label{sec:res-many}

Under the no-storage rule the proposed model beats GB-LAST on S10 for both horizon sets ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<10^{-10}$) and on S7 for $h{=}1$--3 (Fig.~\ref{fig:dash-unseen}b--d; table: supplement Table~SXIV). GB-ALL, which stores every condition, stays better on 52 of 64 S10 and 50 of 60 S7 conditions; its higher S10 mean comes from a few calendar conditions where it fails (up to 17~pp).

\subsection{Bounded memory: the replay ensemble V2}
\label{sec:res-d38}

Keeping 40 rows per condition (post hoc; Fig.~\ref{fig:dash-d38}), V2 shows no replicated difference from the joint TFT and reaches pooled 90\% coverage of 0.89--0.91. It beats extrapolation and the earlier model on S7 and S10 and gradient boosting on S10, but there mostly where boosting fails (median gains 0.02--0.19~pp); coverage drops to 0.81--0.84 on S10 calendar and S7 cyclic conditions.

% V. DISCUSSION and VI. CONCLUSION (shortened on 15 Nov 2026)
% Every number is taken from docs/RESULTS.md and the committed results files.
% ============================================================

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\textbf{Why it works.} Building on the best simple forecaster mattered most: extrapolation fails on new conditions, gradient boosting forgets on the stream, and the residual model inherits extrapolation's stability while learning condition effects (Figs.~\ref{fig:overview}, \ref{fig:dash-s6}a,b). Most of the remaining gap to GB-ALL and joint training comes from storing data, not from the model: with 40 rows per condition, V2 matches joint training. Continual learning therefore suits data that cannot be kept (privacy, ownership, volume).

\textbf{Reuse.} The classes screen on relative capacity only; power, safety, absolute capacity and cost also matter. For a group unlike any seen before (condition~7, Figs.~\ref{fig:dash-s6}d, \ref{fig:dash-unseen}a), neither forecasts nor intervals can be trusted, and pooled coverage hides it.

\textbf{Limitations.} We switched to forecasting after seeing S1, and all follow-ups came after the main results (registered except the ablation; the GB stream test and V2 are post hoc, and S7/S10 were added to find a setting where the model wins). Second-life sets are small, S6 is aged at 50~$^\circ$C, SOH is relative to the first check, and planned usage is assumed known.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Residual TFT-EWC forecasts second-life SOH as a shrunk correction to linear extrapolation and is the only model compared that holds up both on a continual stream and on unseen conditions, including all 64 S10 conditions against gradient boosting under the same no-storage rule. Models that store all earlier data remain more accurate; a small replay memory closes most of that gap. Intervals hold only when calibrated on held-out conditions within the training range. Future work: larger groups whose data cannot be stored, and power and safety criteria for screening.
